# naxp

<!-- badges: start -->
[![R-CMD-check](https://github.com/logmu-org/r-naxp/actions/workflows/R-CMD-check.yaml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/logmu-org/r-naxp/actions/workflows/R-CMD-check.yaml)
[![Lifecycle: experimental](https://img.shields.io/badge/lifecycle-experimental-orange.svg)](https://lifecycle.r-lib.org/articles/stages.html#experimental)
<!-- badges: end -->

Dealing with postcodes, flight numbers and other alphanumeric data codes
is a common problem. Handling strings is cumbersome and
the codes themselves can often be written in multiple different ways
&ndash; for instance `EC1A1BB` and `EC1A 1BB` are the same UK postcode.

A **naxp** ('encoded ASCII expression') simplifies this by
encoding each distinct alphanumeric data code as an integer.

With a **naxp**, you define the code system
once using a flexible regex-like syntax, and then you're done.
Every **naxp** library, in every language (R, C, C++, C# and JavaScript), produces exactly the same encoding,
which means that the encoded values are safe
to store in files,
to use in databases, and
to pass between different programs
written in different languages.
And, as an added bonus, integers are more performant than strings.

The [**naxp** website](https://naxp.org/) provides everything you need
to understand and write **naxp**s:

- A good place to start is the
[**naxp** quick tour](https://naxp.org/#quick-tour).

- For common use cases, there are built-in
[standard **naxp**s](https://naxp.org/standard/),
which can be accessed direct from the R `naxp` package.

- The site also has an
[interactive **naxp** design tool](https://naxp.org/interactive/)
and a [**naxp** migration tester](https://naxp.org/migrate/).

## Installation

Install from CRAN:

```r
install.packages("naxp")
```

Or install the latest development version from GitHub:

```r
# install.packages("pak")
pak::pak("logmu-org/r-naxp")
```

## Example


```{r}
library(naxp)

# Assume we have some UK postcodes
postcodes_as_text <- c(
  "CR2 6XH",
  "DN55 1PT",
  "M1 1AE",
  "EC1A1BB", # The mandated space is sometimes omitted
  "not a postcode")

# UK postcodes are complicated so let's grab the standard naxp
postcode_naxp <- naxp_standard("uk-postcode")
postcode_naxp

# Encode the text postcodes
postcodes <- naxp_encode(postcodes_as_text, postcode_naxp)

# The encoded result looks like text ...
postcodes

# ... but the underlying values are numerical,
# with 0 (not NA!) representing invalid text.
as.integer(postcodes)

# We can recover the canonical text form at any time.
# 0 (invalid text) decodes to NA.
naxp_decode(postcodes)
```
